idiom_name: one well-known key-to-entry table + register/lookup operations over it
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: pick a single, well-advertised object or module to own a key-to-entry table; expose exactly two operations over it - register(key, entry-or-factory) and lookup(key) - and decide the policy questions once, in that object: which key type is legal, what happens on duplicate registration, whether entries are instances or factories, when registration may happen (start-up only or at runtime) and how concurrent register/lookup are made safe. Advertise the registry through the narrowest surface that works (one module, one injected instance) rather than a global bag, and give tests a way to install a fresh registry or clear it. Add listing/diagnostics only if the host genuinely needs to enumerate what is available.
code_sketch:
registry = well_known_table()          # one owner, one key domain
registry.register(key, factory)      # fail fast on duplicate keys
entry = registry.lookup(key)          # or raise/error on unknown key
# policy decided once: key type, duplicate handling, laziness,
lifetimes, thread-safety, reset-for-tests
pitfalls: Skipping the policy decisions: without duplicate handling and a lifetime rule the registry silently becomes an unordered global dump.
Letting entries be looked up by convention (stringly-typed keys) with no validation, so typos surface as 'unknown key' at runtime.
Exposing the whole table for outside mutation instead of register/lookup operations, which forfeits encapsulation and duplicate detection.

Using a registry as a universal service locator: callers gain hidden dependencies and missing keys fail at runtime -> instead inject required interfaces at component boundaries and confine global lookup to composition or bootstrap code.

Relying on import-time or class-loading side effects with no explicit discovery order: duplicate or missing providers then depend on load order -> instead make registration a deliberate bootstrap phase and fail fast with diagnostics before serving requests.
